questions.stem: Which multiplication has the same answer as 2 + 2 + 2 + 2?
questions.stemText: Which multiplication has the same answer as 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 ?
questions.explain: Count the 2s: there are 4 of them, so this is 4 groups of 2, which is 4 × 2 = 8. Counting one group too many gives 5 × 2, which is 2 too much, and multiplying the wrong pair gives 2 × 2 or 5 × 4. Multiplication is a short way of writing the same number added over and over - that is the whole idea, and it is why the times tables are worth knowing by heart.

questions.stem: Jun Hao works out 2711 + 6683 in columns. One column makes 13, so he writes 3 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 3 he writes there worth?
questions.stemText: Jun Hao works out 2711 + 6683 in columns. One column makes 13, so he writes 3 in that column and a small 1 above the column on its left. How much is the 3 he writes there worth?
questions.explain: The column that makes 13 is the hundreds column: 7 + 6 = 13, and no other column reaches ten. 13 hundreds is 1 thousand and 3 hundreds, so the 3 stays in the hundreds column - worth 300 - and the small 1 goes above the thousands column - worth 1000. The 3 is worth 300. A mark is worth the column it is written in, not the digit it looks like: that is what regrouping means, ten of something small becoming one of the next size up. Every wrong answer here is one of the two slips - the right digit read in the wrong column, or the wrong digit read in the right one.

questions.stem: Xin Yi works out 61 + 66 in her head. She makes 70 first. 61 + 66 = 70 + ?
questions.stemText: Xin Yi works out 61 + 66 in her head. She makes 70 first. 61 + 66 = 70 + ?
questions.explain: To get from 61 up to 70 you need 9, so 9 is moved across from the 66. That leaves 66 − 9 = 57, and 70 + 57 = 127. Whatever you give to one number you must take off the other, or the total changes. You could have rounded the 66 up to 70 instead and taken that amount off the 61: it is the same total either way, so it lands on the same answer.

questions.stem: A rectangular banner is 15 cm long and 10 cm wide. A notch 5 cm wide and 3 cm deep is cut out of the middle of one long side, so the notch does not reach either end. Along that side there is 6 cm of edge before the notch and 4 cm after it, and the banner is still 7 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.stemText: A rectangular banner is 15 cm long and 10 cm wide. A notch 5 cm wide and 3 cm deep is cut out of the middle of one long side, so the notch does not reach either end. Along that side there is 6 cm of edge before the notch and 4 cm after it, and the banner is still 7 cm wide behind the notch. Every corner is a right angle. What is the perimeter of the banner now?
questions.explain: Walk the eight sides: 6 + 3 + 5 + 3 + 4 + 10 + 15 + 10 = 56 cm. Careful: this notch is in the middle of a side, not at a corner. The 5 cm taken out of the top edge is replaced by the 5 cm along the bottom of the notch, so that part of the walk is unchanged. But the two sides of the notch, 3 cm down and 3 cm back up, are brand new. Perimeter = 2 × (15 + 10) + 2 × 3 = 56 cm. A corner cut leaves the perimeter alone; a middle notch makes it longer.
